notes: Reinforcement learning with a single adaptive biologically plausible reward learns locomotion controllers for four musculoskeletal models (up to 90 muscles) in two simulators without any motion demonstrations; the controllers generalize to diverse unseen terrains and remain robust on complex 3D models where reflex controllers are difficult to apply, producing close-to-natural gait.
robot_sim: Implement RL with the adaptive biologically plausible reward on a musculoskeletal biped as an alternative to hand-tuned reflex/CPG hierarchies; benchmark terrain generalization and muscle-count scalability against reflex-based controllers.

notes: Review of interlimb coordination in mammalian locomotion: coordination between forelimb and hindlimb spinal networks is achieved by mechanisms intrinsic to the spinal cord, somatosensory feedback from the limbs, and supraspinal pathways; incomplete spinal cord injury disrupts this coordination, but lesion-based inference is confounded by compensatory strategies, redundant control, and plasticity in remaining circuits.
animal_study: Dissociate the intrinsic-spinal, somatosensory, and supraspinal contributions to interlimb coordination by combining selective spinal lesions with acute pre-plasticity recordings across gaits and voluntary limb-use tasks, directly addressing the compensation and redundancy confounds the review identifies.
robot_sim: Build a locomotion model with separate interlimb-coupling modules (intraspinal coupling, limb somatosensory feedback, supraspinal modulation) and ablate them individually to reproduce the coordination disruptions seen after incomplete spinal lesions.

notes: Brief trains to flexor reflex afferents (FRA: joint, cutaneous, group II-III muscle afferents) reset the L-dopa-induced fictive locomotor rhythm in high-spinal cats - interrupting extensor activity and initiating flexion when delivered in extension, or prolonging flexion in late flexion - demonstrating that FRA interneurones are constituent elements of the rhythm-generating network organized along half-centre lines.
animal_study: Re-test FRA resetting in an intact walking preparation by phase-locked stimulation of group II and cutaneous afferents, quantifying reset versus entrainment, to check that the curarized L-dopa result generalizes to freely walking animals.
robot_sim: Implement FRA input as a phase-dependent reset of the half-centre oscillator (extensor interruption plus flexion trigger, flexion prolongation late in flexion) and verify that brief afferent trains shorten or lengthen single cycles after which the original rhythm period resumes.
flags: FRA-train reset of the rhythm (flexion-pattern reset interrupting extension) fits no exact feedback vocabulary term; candidate 'FRA resets step cycle'. Abstract also names joint afferents (no vocabulary entry) and extension-prolonging group I effects (Ia vs Ib unspecified).

notes: Across downslope grades (25-100%) in walking cats, stance-phase yield increases at the ankle, swing-phase knee and ankle flexion decreases while ankle extension lowers the paw to contact, hip extensors fall silent and hip flexors instead brake the rate of hip extension, and ankle extensor bursts truncate around paw contact - a systematic reorganization of the motor pattern to counteract external braking forces rather than a rescaled level-gait pattern.
animal_study: Record hindlimb afferent activity (spindle and tendon organ) during graded downslope walking to identify which feedback signals track the slope-dependent reorganization of hip and ankle extensor activity that the kinematic/EMG analysis reveals.
robot_sim: Gate hip extensor stance drive off and engage hip flexors as mid-stance brakes on downslope terrain, with ankle extensor bursts truncated around paw contact, and test whether a fixed CPG plus slope-dependent gating reproduces the measured downslope kinematics.

notes: Review synthesizing that locomotor recovery through treadmill training in spinalized cats and spinal-cord-injured patients rests on a spinal central pattern generator whose activation and regulation depend on locomotor-related afferent input: adequate sensory input during training can drive and calibrate the spinal locomotor circuitry, a principle for designing gait rehabilitation programs.
animal_study: Systematically vary the sensory content of treadmill training (loading, limb-loading timing, cutaneous input) in spinalized cats to identify which locomotor-related afferent signals most effectively activate and regulate the spinal pattern generator.
robot_sim: Implement a CPG controller whose activation and phase regulation are gated by locomotor-related afferent input, and ablate that input to show that training-like recovery of rhythmic output fails under tonic drive alone.

notes: Early legged-vehicle control work introducing automatic body-regulation schemes built on an improved stability measure that can be optimized automatically, combined with the kinematic limits of individual legs, to maintain stability and maneuverability on highly irregular terrain while reducing operator burden.
robot_sim: Use an automatically optimized stability margin subject to per-leg kinematic limits as a body-height and posture regulator for a rough-terrain walker - a non-neural benchmark against which to compare vestibular- and reflex-based balance controllers.

notes: For two weakly coupled neural oscillators, shared (correlated) noise can induce bistability between synchronous and anti-phase states even when anti-phase is the only stable state without noise; an asymptotic Fokker-Planck reduction (rho(0)) is far cheaper than Monte-Carlo or 2D solvers and accurately predicts a synaptically coupled Morris-Lecar system.
animal_study: Apply shared versus independent stochastic stimulation to two biological rhythm-generating circuits (e.g., isolated hemicords) and test whether correlated input alone produces bistable synchronous/anti-phase locking, as the theory predicts.
robot_sim: Inject correlated sensory noise into two weakly coupled half-centre oscillators to verify noise-induced bistability between synchrony and anti-phase, and use the rho(0) phase reduction in place of Monte-Carlo simulation for parameter sweeps.

notes: Chronic dorsal-root recordings of spindle primary afferents in freely moving cats showed that fusimotor drive to ankle extensors operates mainly in the extension phases of stepping, that unexpected loading (back thrust) evokes a potent fusimotor response, and that during falls Ia discharge decreases despite rising extensor EMG - clear evidence for independent alpha and gamma control - while clonus-like paw-shaking belongs to the normal motor repertoire.
animal_study: Replicate with simultaneous Ia (and II) afferent, muscle-length, and force recordings during overground stepping and sudden loading to quantify the phase-timing of fusimotor drive and the alpha-gamma dissociation during falls.
robot_sim: Model fusimotor action as a phase-gated gain on spindle feedback - raised in extension, boosted by load transients, suppressed during falls - and test whether state-dependent afferent gain improves load compensation in a walking controller.

notes: Adaptive frequency oscillators automatically tune their intrinsic frequency to the resonant frequency of a compliant quadruped robot using only local sensory feedback; the learned frequency persists after the robot halts and re-adapts when body mass changes, with a linearized convergence analysis identifying which sensory feedback types support stable adaptation.
animal_study: Test whether locomotor frequency re-tunes after body-mass changes during growth in developing animals, as the adaptive-frequency account predicts from the robot's re-adaptation to mass changes.
robot_sim: Couple adaptive frequency oscillators to a compliant locomotion plant so intrinsic frequency tracks plant resonance via local feedback; verify persistence of the learned frequency at halt and re-adaptation after a mass change.

notes: A spinal circuit model with asymmetric cervical-lumbar layout (V0D versus V0V commissural interneurons mediating left-right alternation at the two levels) reproduces quadruped walk/trot, half-bound after V0V deletion, bound after V0 deletion, unilateral versus bilateral scratching after V0V deletion, and afferent-plus-perineal-driven coordination in backward-biped-spinal locomotion - supporting one shared spinal network reconfigured by supraspinal input and somatosensory feedback across motor behaviors.
animal_study: Test the model's ablation predictions by selectively silencing V0V and combined V0 commissural populations and quantifying the predicted gait changes (trot to half-bound/bound) and bilateral scratching synchrony, plus perineal/afferent-driven backward stepping.
robot_sim: Implement the asymmetric cervical-lumbar CIN network in a quadruped simulator; ablate V0V then V0D+V0V to check the gait transitions, and drive network reconfiguration with afferent feedback plus perineal-like stimulation to switch among forward, backward, and scratching modes.

notes: Measured the loop gain of homonymous positive force feedback from ankle extensor Golgi tendon organs in decerebrate walking cats: about 0.2 at short muscle lengths (roughly 20 percent of total activity and force) rising to 0.5 at long lengths (about 50 percent), with the length dependence arising from the intrinsic force-length property while the force-to-motoneuron gain stays length-independent - establishing positive Ib feedback as a substantial contributor to stance extensor drive, not a minor modulator.
animal_study: Test whether Ib loop gain remains in the 0.2-0.5 range across speed and slope in intact walking cats, and whether selectively removing tendon-organ feedback reduces extensor force by the predicted 20-50 percent.
robot_sim: Implement homonymous positive force feedback on stance extensors with loop gain 0.2-0.5, scaled by the muscle force-length property; ablating it should cut extensor activity by a length-dependent 20-50 percent.

notes: Review arguing that spinal central pattern generator networks are an experimentally tractable model system for understanding how moderately complex neuronal ensembles generate specific motor behaviors, and that novel molecular-genetic tools plus advances in knowledge of spinal cord development bring a comprehensive circuit-level account of locomotor organization within reach.
animal_study: Use genetic ablation or silencing of identified spinal interneuron populations during locomotion to assign each class a role in rhythm versus pattern generation.
robot_sim: Build CPG models whose components correspond to genetically identified interneuron classes and delete classes one at a time to compare simulated phenotypes with mutant locomotion.

notes: Review of the rhythmogenic core of the mammalian locomotor CPG: genetic approaches have identified spinal interneuron populations and their roles in stepping, but the identity and interconnection of the rhythm-generating neurons themselves remain undeciphered; compiles the properties expected of rhythmogenic neurons and the candidate genetically defined classes.
animal_study: Silence candidate rhythmogenic interneuron classes during fictive locomotion and test whether rhythm (as opposed to pattern) collapses, using the review's compiled feature list of rhythm-generating neurons as selection criteria.
robot_sim: Construct a CPG whose rhythmogenic kernel exhibits the expected rhythm-neuron features alongside separate pattern circuitry; ablate candidate kernel classes to test which removal stops rhythm generation while leaving patterning intact.

notes: A full-muscle 3D rat hindlimb model driven by physiological walking data shows that muscle moment arms depend strongly on the configuration of adjacent joints - critical for biarticular torque computation - and that moment-arm profiles vary enough across the step cycle to imply changes in muscle function during walking.
animal_study: Validate the predicted moment-arm profiles against in vivo tendon-excursion or bone-pin kinematic measurements in walking rats, particularly for biarticular muscles whose arms depend on adjacent-joint configuration.
robot_sim: Derive muscle moment arms from 3D attachment points with adjacent-joint dependence when mapping muscle force to joint torque in rat-scale (or scaled) locomotion models; ignoring the adjacent-joint term misestimates biarticular torques.

notes: Per the abstract provided: across steep downslope grades in walking cats, stance-phase yield increases at the ankle, swing knee and ankle flexion decreases with ankle extension lowering the paw to contact, hip extensors fall silent while hip flexors brake the rate of hip extension, and ankle extensor bursts truncate around paw contact - the motor pattern reorganizes to counteract external braking forces rather than simply rescaling level gait.
animal_study: Record hindlimb proprioceptive afferents during graded downslope walking to identify feedback signals associated with the disappearance of hip extensor activity and truncation of ankle extensor bursts.
robot_sim: Gate hip extensor drive off and use hip flexors as stance brakes on downslopes, with ankle extensor bursts centered on paw contact, testing whether a fixed CPG with slope-dependent gating reproduces the graded downslope kinematics.
flags: Abstract is identical to Smith 1998 'Forms III' (downslope) despite the title reading 'II ... upslope and level walking' - likely a metadata/abstract swap; replace with the true upslope abstract before relying on upslope-specific conclusions.

notes: Review concluding that locomotor recovery after spinal lesions in adult mammals is partly due to plasticity within existing spinal locomotor networks: locomotor training changes the excitability of simple reflex pathways and more complex circuitry, adaptation to lesions entails changes at both spinal and supraspinal levels, and the cat-derived framework extends to rat, mouse, and human spinal pattern generation.
animal_study: Record reflex excitability and locomotor patterns before and after standardized lesions, with and without training, in cats to separate plasticity within remaining spinal circuits from regeneration- or supraspinal-mediated recovery.
robot_sim: Model lesion and recovery by removing pathways and re-tuning residual connection weights through training-like afferent input, testing which plasticity rules restore stepping when descending drive is lost.

notes: Isolated red muscle bundles driven through the in vivo length changes and stimulation patterns of steady swimming showed that most swimming power comes from posterior musculature while the anterior mainly transmits force - the opposite of the prevailing assumption - and that contractile properties are regionally tuned along the body to enhance power production.
animal_study: Apply the isolated work-loop paradigm at multiple body locations in additional species to map regional power generation versus force transmission along the musculature.
robot_sim: In undulatory swimmer models, assign posterior-dominant power production with rostral force transmission and regionally tuned contractile properties instead of uniform actuation, and quantify the effect on swimming performance.
flags: Abstract says only 'fish' (no species); animals mapped to the closest allowed bucket 'Vertebrates' - consider adding 'Fish' to the vocabulary.

notes: Self-reinnervation of cat gastrocnemius muscles (motor function recovers, proprioceptive feedback permanently absent) leaves level- and upslope-walking kinematics recovered within 14-19 weeks but produces permanent ankle and interjoint deficits in downslope walking - indicating MG/LG proprioceptive feedback is specifically required for regulating ankle extensors on downslope, with compensation by other sensory sources (e.g., cutaneous) or altered central drive elsewhere.
animal_study: Combine MG/LG self-reinnervation with graded cutaneous anesthesia during downslope walking to test whether cutaneous input is the compensating sensory source for the lost muscle proprioception.
robot_sim: Ablate length and force feedback from ankle extensors in a slope-walking simulator: level and upslope gaits should tolerate the loss via central-drive/cutaneous compensation while downslope develops persistent ankle yield - a test of feedback redundancy.
flags: 'Length feedback' from MG/LG mapped to spindle Ia/II (reinnervation also silences Ib); Cutaneous included because the abstract names it explicitly.

notes: In mice with glutamatergic neurotransmission ablated from the spinal locomotor region, inhibitory interneuron networks alone generate locomotor-like rhythmicity, and flexor-extensor alternation is produced by Ia inhibitory interneurons - the proprioceptive reciprocal-inhibition pathway - defining a minimal inhibitory network sufficient for locomotor pattern generation.
animal_study: Silence Ia inhibitory interneurons on top of the glutamate ablation and test whether flexor-extensor alternation is abolished while rhythmic bursting persists, completing the sufficiency/necessity test.
robot_sim: Model antagonist motoneuron pools connected through reciprocally inhibiting Ia inhibitory interneurons; ablating the Ia inhibitory population should collapse alternation into co-contraction.

notes: Four general principles of CPG rhythmogenesis: rhythmogenic ionic currents underlie every CPG regardless of network-pacemaker versus endogenous-kernel organization; fast synaptic transmission can evoke slow currents that alter cycle frequency; rhythmogenesis is multiply and redundantly implemented; and glial cells may participate - with CPGs able to drive rhythmic behavior without sensory feedback while afferents modulate cycle frequency and phase timing.
animal_study: Sequentially block candidate ionic currents and synaptic pathways in an isolated CPG preparation and measure rhythm persistence, to test the redundancy principle directly.
robot_sim: Build CPG neurons with coexisting rhythmogenic mechanisms (intrinsic currents, network reciprocity, slow synaptic currents) and ablate them one at a time - reproducing why single-mechanism lesions typically fail to abolish rhythm.

notes: A minimalist quadruped robot controlled by four decoupled oscillators with only local force feedback in each leg reproduces animal-like walking patterns and adapts to changes in weight distribution and walking speed - evidence that physical (mechanically mediated) interlimb communication, not dedicated neural coupling, can suffice for interlimb coordination.
animal_study: Test whether quadrupeds with severed intraspinal commissural pathways still show mechanically mediated interlimb coordination through ground reaction forces, as the local-feedback-only account predicts.
robot_sim: Implement decoupled per-leg oscillators coordinated solely by local ground-force feedback (no inter-oscillator neural coupling) and verify gait emergence and adaptation to load redistribution; ablate the force feedback to show coordination collapses.
flags: Robot's sole coordinating signal is local per-leg force feedback (mechanosensory analog) - no exact feedback vocabulary term; candidate 'local leg force feedback'.

notes: During fictive locomotion in decerebrate cats, group I stimulation evokes locomotor-dependent disynaptic excitation (single interneurone, mean latency 1.64 ms) of most flexor (89 percent) and many bifunctional (64 percent) motoneurones, largest during flexion and from homonymous nerves, evoked by both tendon-organ (Ib) and muscle-spindle (Ia) afferents and separate from the extensor group I pathway - indicating distinct flexor and extensor excitatory interneurone groups that reinforce ongoing locomotor activity throughout the limb.
animal_study: Identify and label the flexor-projecting group I excitatory interneurones during fictive locomotion and test their phase modulation in intact walking to confirm the separate flexor versus extensor interneurone groups.
robot_sim: Add disynaptic group I excitation of flexor and bifunctional motoneurone pools, phase-weighted to peak during flexion and driven by homonymous afferents, as load-reinforcement of ongoing activity; ablate it to quantify the loss of flexor reinforcement.
flags: Also shows Ia spindle afferents evoking DISYNAPTIC excitation of flexor motoneurones - 'Ia monosynaptic excitation' does not fit; candidate vocabulary term 'Ia disynaptic excitation (flexors)'.

notes: Review of adaptive interlimb coordination in legged robots: coordination arises from dynamic interactions among the neural system, the musculoskeletal system, and the environment; it is reshaped by locomotion speed, environmental situation, body properties, and task, and exhibits characteristic properties such as gait hysteresis and adaptation on different time scales - principles used to design bio-inspired robot control from neurophysiological sensorimotor findings.
animal_study: Measure gait-transition hysteresis and the time-scale separation of interlimb adaptations in walking animals across speed ramps, to compare animal and robot coordination properties directly.
robot_sim: Incorporate gait hysteresis and multiple adaptation time scales into the interlimb-coordination layer of legged-robot controllers when implementing speed-, body-, and task-dependent gait changes.

notes: Multidisciplinary review arguing that electrically activating spinal interneuronal circuits (reflex and pattern-generating) could coordinate many muscles at once for neuroprostheses, far more tractable than stimulating each muscle individually; draws on phase-adaptable cat hindlimb reflexes, chick embryo rhythmogenic network development, the cat spinal locomotor pattern generator, and locomotor training in incomplete SCI patients to identify candidate circuits and the control problems engineers must solve.
animal_study: In spinal cats, test circuit-level stimulation strategies that exploit phase-dependent modulation of reflex pathways to augment stepping, as a preclinical step toward functional neuromuscular stimulation in humans.
robot_sim: Model the control layer for FNS-style stimulation as a spinal circuit hierarchy (phase-modulated reflexes plus CPG) driving a musculoskeletal limb, instead of per-muscle open-loop stimulation.
flags: Chick embryo rhythmogenesis is discussed but 'Bird/Chick' is absent from the animals vocabulary - mapped to 'Vertebrates'; consider adding.

notes: Continuous conductance measurements from neonatal mouse motoneurones during locomotor-like activity show push-pull CPG operation (alternating excitatory and inhibitory conductances with inhibitory predominance, most pronounced in extensors), sharper phase tuning of flexor-related than extensor-related synaptic drives, and rostral-versus-caudal segmental differences - evidence for reciprocally coupled but differently composed flexor and extensor modules in a multilayered, distributed premotor network, preserved across frequencies and drug combinations.
animal_study: Test the rostral/caudal CPG asymmetry with segment-specific recordings or lesions of the isolated cord, and verify the extensor-dominant inhibition with identified premotor interneurone recordings during locomotor-like activity.
robot_sim: Implement premotor modules as reciprocally coupled flexor and extensor half-centers with unequal phase-tuning sharpness, inhibition-dominant extensor drive, and rostral/caudal parameter differences, then compare generated motoneurone conductance profiles with the extracted ones.
